narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 63.0% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means the risk was judged higher than the chance of passing, not that failure was certain. The decision was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the fifth or sixth decile. That was the single strongest signal pushing the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 22, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37, was the second strongest signal and also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor, but it actually worked in your favor: a third-decile position was below the accepted average of about sixth decile, yet it still pushed the estimate toward passing rather than failing. It was not enough to offset the third-year and LSAT concerns. To move forward, focus on strengthening the areas the model weighted most: seek academic advising and support for your third-year record, and prepare intensively to retake the LSAT if law school remains your goal. Then consult an admissions advisor about reapplying with improved credentials and a clear explanation of your progress.
